video.title: Why Pros Hit So Far Away

classification.reason: The coach provides actionable drills and cues such as holding a cone or weight in the non-hitting hand and doing stationary lunging swings to calibrate contact spacing.

problem.title_as_question: Why do pros hit the forehand so far away from their body?
problem.definition: Players improving their forehand mechanics often intuitively revert to an old, jammed contact point close to the body, which paralyzes the shoulder and disrupts balance and trunk rotation.
prerequisites: shoulder attached swinging through a gentle semicircle
problem.target_player: improving players transitioning from a pushing forehand to advanced rotational mechanics

symptoms.description: The player feels jammed at contact and awkward leaning back to push the ball.
The hitting arm collapses into a chicken wing or gets stuck behind the trunk during forward rotation.
Stroke velocity and trunk coordination noticeably decrease when the non-hitting arm is kept tucked in.
The swing falls off to the left because driving through the heel sends balance backwards.

causes.statement: Players instinctively revert to their old jammed contact lane developed from a pushing forehand habit.
The non-hitting arm is left dangling inside instead of extending across the body to stabilize the trunk and gauge distance.
When contact is too close laterally, the elbow cannot drive in the direction the chest faces and must yank across the body.
Failing to set up sufficient front-to-back depth spacing traps the hitting arm against the trunk during rotation.

angles.summary: Hitting in the correct lateral slot initially feels comically far away to the right compared to an old pushing slot.
Spacing the ball properly allows the elbow pressing vector to align directly with the direction the chest faces.
Preparing for low balls feels like a Romanian deadlift to get the hand comfortably below the ball without lifting with the arm.
Aggressive footwork does not mean crowding the ball; running directly into the ball destroys necessary depth spacing.
Reaching too far in front produces a butt-back, racket-forward posture, which must be countered with patience.

solutions.summary: Hold an object such as a cone in your non-hitting hand during preparation to keep the arm extended and cue spacing.
solutions.external_goal: Hold a cone in your non-hitting hand visible in your peripheral vision.

solutions.summary: Upgrade from holding a cone to holding a 2.5 lb weight in your non-hitting hand to viscerally load trunk stabilization.
solutions.external_goal: Hold a 2.5 lb weight in the non-hitting hand.

solutions.summary: Perform the lunge drill by fixing feet in place, lunging out to probe contact comically far to the right with clean upper body rotation.
solutions.external_goal: Lunge toward balls placed comically far to your right without taking extra adjustment steps.

solutions.summary: On low balls, imagine a Romanian deadlift posture to lower the racket and rotate on a slanted plane rather than lifting with the arm.
When intending to lean forward into an approaching shot, budget extra depth spacing so forward trunk momentum does not jam your arm.
solutions.external_goal: Leave several extra inches of space in front between yourself and the ball before initiating your forward lean.
